opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the nice thing about small boards, like 5x5 or 7x7 or even 9x9, is that the game is short enough that random play actually tells you something. On a 19x19 board, if two players just place stones randomly, the outcome is close to pure noise. The game drags on for hundreds of moves and the final score has almost no relationship to whether your first move was any good. On a tiny board, a random rollout ends in maybe a few dozen moves, so there's some real signal in who wins. If a position is genuinely strong, random continuations from it will win a bit more often than chance.

That's the seed. Monte Carlo tree search doesn't need a good evaluator to start. It just needs an evaluator that's slightly better than a coin flip, because the tree search amplifies it. You run a bunch of random playouts from each candidate move, the moves that win more get explored more, and you build up a tree where the statistics near the root become much sharper than any single noisy rollout. So even with zero knowledge, MCTS plus random rollouts gives you a player that's meaningfully stronger than random.

Then you can bootstrap. You take the games that this search-based player produces and train a policy and value network on them. The value network learns to predict outcomes better than a random rollout, and the policy network learns which moves the search tends to like. Now you plug those back into MCTS: the policy prunes the branches you bother exploring, and the value net replaces or supplements the rollouts. The search gets stronger, it generates better games, you retrain, and you climb. That's basically the AlphaZero loop, but you can watch it happen from scratch on a laptop at small board sizes.

The broader lesson I find really compelling is that you don't need a smart starting point. You need a domain where cheap, dumb exploration gives you a weak but nonzero signal, and a search procedure that can turn that into a stronger signal. Small boards give you that because the horizon is short. Once you have a network that understands local tactics on a small board, you can sometimes carry it over to bigger boards, since a lot of Go is local fighting, capturing, and life and death that looks the same regardless of board size.

I think that's also a useful way to think about bootstrapping in other domains, including language models doing reasoning. The question is always where your first weak signal comes from, and whether you have a search or verification loop that can amplify it without just amplifying your own mistakes.

r002.rationale: It explains that random playout win rates guide MCTS exploration and sharpen root statistics, then describes using the search-generated games to train a policy network.

r003.rationale: The response says MCTS can start without a good evaluator if it has a slightly better-than-chance signal; it does not say MCTS breaks down without grounded value estimates.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that random play is kind of embarrassingly bad as a policy, but it's a surprisingly good value estimator if you average over enough of it. That's the whole insight behind Monte Carlo methods in Go going back to the Brügmann and Coulom stuff. On a 9x9 board, a random rollout takes maybe eighty moves, and you can run thousands of them a second on a laptop. So even though any individual game is nonsense, the statistics of who wins from a given position carry real signal.

And the reason that bootstraps tree search is that MCTS doesn't need a good policy to get started. It just needs some way to score leaves. So you start with uniform random rollouts, you build a tree, and the tree itself starts concentrating simulations on moves that are winning more often. That's the bootstrap: the tree is a better player than the rollout policy, and you can then distill that better player back into the rollout policy, or into a prior over moves, and run the whole thing again. That's basically the loop that AlphaGo Zero made famous, but on small boards you can watch it happen in an afternoon with no neural network at all.

The reason I like small boards specifically is that the branching factor is small enough that random rollouts actually reach terminal states with meaningful outcomes. On 19x19, random play is so far from anything a real game looks like that the value estimates are almost noise. On 5x5 or 7x7, the game is short enough that random play covers a decent chunk of the relevant state space, and you can see the tree discover things like "don't fill your own eyes" purely from win statistics, without anyone hand-coding it.

What I find kind of philosophically interesting is that it's a case where search substitutes for knowledge. You have zero prior about the game, and compute plus a correct reward signal gets you to a reasonable player. And then once you have that player, you can amortize it into a learned prior, and now the search is cheaper. I think that pattern, where a dumb-but-correct process bootstraps a smart-but-approximate one, shows up all over the place in robotics and RL, and Go on a small board is the cleanest toy version of it I know.

r001.rationale: The response calls individual random games “nonsense” and says random play is a bad policy; it does not claim random play produces reasonable, human-like board positions.

r002.rationale: It explains that random rollouts score search leaves through win statistics, allowing MCTS to concentrate simulations on winning moves and improve the player.

r003.rationale: It says MCTS needs a way to score leaves and describes rollout outcomes as the value signal, communicating that search needs grounded scoring to guide it.

astra-6.text:
The key is that a random game can be a terrible game of Go and still give you a little bit of information about which position is better. On a small board, you can play lots of those games cheaply, and they terminate quickly enough that you get a win or a loss.

So, for each candidate move, you run a bunch of random continuations and estimate how often you win. Those estimates are noisy, and winning against random play isn’t the same as winning against a strong opponent. But if there’s enough signal to favor some moves over others, you’ve already got something better than choosing randomly.

Monte Carlo tree search then allocates more computation to promising branches while still exploring alternatives. As the tree grows, more of the important decisions are made by search, and the random rollout gets pushed further toward the end of the game.

And if you train a policy on the moves that search selects, you can get a feedback loop: a slightly better policy makes search more effective, and better search generates better training targets. The small board makes that initial bootstrap easier because the gap between a random action and an observable outcome is much shorter.

r001.rationale: The response says random games can be poor and yield noisy win/loss signals; it does not say they produce reasonable, human-like board positions.

r002.rationale: It explains estimating win rates from random continuations for candidate moves, using those estimates to favor moves in search, and training on search-selected moves to improve the policy.

r003.rationale: It does not state that MCTS breaks down without grounded value estimates; it says noisy random-rollout outcomes can still provide enough signal to guide search.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that a random rollout can be a very weak signal and still be useful. Take a candidate move, play a bunch of random games from that position, and ask how often you win. On a small Go board, the games are short enough that you can do this a lot, and the consequences of a good or bad move show up relatively quickly.

Then tree search gives you this feedback loop. You spend more simulations on moves that look promising, while still exploring alternatives. As the tree gets deeper, more of each simulated game is determined by the search rather than random play. So you start with a terrible policy, but you progressively replace parts of it with better decisions.

There’s a caveat: you’re initially estimating how good a move is when followed by random play, which isn’t necessarily how good it is against a strong opponent. But it can give you enough signal to get started. And if you train a policy on the moves selected by search, that policy can guide the next round of search, giving you another improvement loop.

r002.rationale: It explains that repeated random rollouts estimate candidate moves by win rate, that search increasingly selects promising moves, and that training on search-selected moves can improve the policy for later search.

r003.rationale: It mentions a caveat about random-play estimates differing from performance against a strong opponent, but does not state that MCTS breaks down without grounded value estimates.
